title: Cellular Respiration
seo_title: Grade 11 Life Sciences: Cellular Respiration Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_text: Aerobic respiration: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain; the role of mitochondria and ATP; anaerobic respiration in plants and animals (alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation); uses of anaerobic respiration in industry. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 11, Life Sciences: Cellular respiration)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): aerobic respiration, glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, ATP, anaerobic respiration and fermentation. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy.
body_html:
How to think about it

Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose, which is stored in ATP. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into pyruvate; in aerobic respiration the pyruvate enters the mitochondria, where the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain produce most of the ATP, carbon dioxide and water.

Without oxygen, cells respire anaerobically. In muscles, pyruvate becomes lactic acid, causing fatigue. In yeast, it becomes ethanol and carbon dioxide (alcoholic fermentation), which is used to make bread and beer.

Example

Where does the Krebs cycle happen?

The powerhouse of the cell

Answer: in the mitochondria

Example

What does yeast make in anaerobic respiration?

Fermentation

Answer: ethanol and carbon dioxide

Common mistakes

  • Thinking respiration is the same as breathing.
  • Thinking plants do not respire.
  • Thinking anaerobic respiration makes more energy.

faq.a: Yeast respires and releases carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in the dough.

faq.q: Why do you breathe hard after a race?
faq.a: To supply oxygen to break down the lactic acid (the oxygen debt).

items.q: What happens in the link reaction?
c: pyruvate is oxidised to acetyl CoA, releasing CO₂ and reducing NAD
items.e: It takes place in the matrix.

items.q: An organism takes in 36 cm³ of oxygen and gives out 25 cm³ of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
items.e: RQ = CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in = 0,694 (1,0 for carbohydrate, about 0,7 for lipid, about 0,9 for protein).

items.q: What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?
items.e: It forms water.

items.q: What is the role of NAD in respiration?
c: it carries hydrogen (protons and electrons) to the electron transfer chain
items.e: It is reduced in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.

items.q: What is the role of ATP in cells?
c: it is the main component of membranes
it carries energy from respiration to reactions that need it
items.e: ATP → ADP + Pi releases energy.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 10 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 20 ATP.

items.q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
c: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in light, with chlorophyll)
items.e: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 3 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 6 ATP.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 5 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 5 = 10.

items.q: What is the end product of glycolysis?
items.e: Glucose → 2 pyruvic acid.

items.q: Which is used in respiration if carbohydrates run out?
items.e: Fats enter as acetyl CoA, proteins as amino acids.

items.q: What do the light-dependent reactions supply to the Calvin cycle?
items.e: Water is split and oxygen is released.

items.q: An organism takes in 80 cm³ of oxygen and gives out 56 cm³ of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
items.e: RQ = CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in = 0,700 (1,0 for carbohydrate, about 0,7 for lipid, about 0,9 for protein).

items.q: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
c: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ ATP)
items.e: It releases energy as ATP.

items.q: What are cristae?
c: folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane
items.e: They give a large surface area for the electron transfer chain.

items.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in mammals?
items.e: Pyruvate is reduced, regenerating NAD.

items.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction rise between 10 °C and 35 °C?
c: molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme–substrate collisions are more frequent
items.e: Above the optimum, denaturation takes over.

items.q: What happens in human muscles during heavy exercise when oxygen is short?
c: pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid
items.e: This causes fatigue.

items.q: What is a limiting factor?
c: the factor that is present in excess
the factor that is in shortest supply and so controls the rate
a factor that stops a reaction for ever
the temperature at which an enzyme denatures
items.e: Light, CO₂ and temperature limit photosynthesis.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose?
items.e: 4 are made but 2 are used.

items.q: Where does the electron transport chain of aerobic respiration take place?
c: on the inner membrane (cristae) of the mitochondrion
items.e: Most ATP is made here.

items.q: Where does the oxygen given out in photosynthesis come from?
items.e: Shown with heavy-oxygen isotopes.

items.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) of carbohydrates?
items.e: CO₂ given out = O₂ taken in.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 4 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 4 = 8.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 5 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 10 ATP.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 10 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 10 = 20.

items.q: What is the name for the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP?
items.e: RuBisCO: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP.

items.q: What is the first product of the Krebs cycle?
items.e: Acetyl CoA + oxaloacetic acid → citric acid.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 8 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 8 = 16.

items.q: Where in the cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
items.e: The Krebs cycle: the mitochondrial matrix.

items.q: Where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
c: on the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast
items.e: Chlorophyll is in the thylakoids.

items.q: Who showed that sunlight is needed for plants to purify air?
items.e: He used an aquatic plant in light and dark.

items.q: Which factor would NOT increase the rate of photosynthesis in a plant already in bright light at 25 °C with low CO₂?
c: a slightly warmer temperature up to the optimum
items.e: When CO₂ is limiting, extra light makes no difference.

items.q: What is the RQ of fats such as tripalmitin?
items.e: Fats need more oxygen to burn.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) take place?
c: in the stroma of the chloroplast
items.e: CO₂ is fixed by the enzyme RuBisCO.

items.q: Who showed with a bell jar, a mouse and a candle that plants restore 'bad' air?
What happens to an enzyme at a very high temperature?
c: it is denatured: the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits
items.e: Bonds holding the shape break.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 6 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 6 = 12.

items.q: What is Kranz anatomy?
c: a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700)
the enzyme that fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells of C₄ plants
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 680 nm (P680)
large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves
items.e: Kranz anatomy: large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves.

items.q: What is formed when pyruvate enters the mitochondrion?
c: acetyl CoA, with release of CO₂ and NADH
items.e: This is oxidative decarboxylation.

items.q: How many turns of the Krebs cycle are needed to oxidise 9 molecules of glucose completely?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 acetyl CoA, so 2 turns: 18.

items.q: Why is respiration called an amphibolic pathway?

it is used both for breaking down and for building molecules
items.e: Intermediates are used to make fats and proteins.
